name: Dana Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign for any side, and this conversation is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Dana, 58, an experienced electrician with a vocational certificate and an electrician's licence. I'm about average at the work, usually finding an awkward connection in a shop or fitting replacement lights in somebody's house, rather than running a crew. I like leaving the covers straight and the customer knowing what was done. I use AI now and then for a checked explanation after somebody has shown me a useful example, but the electrical checks still belong to me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is waiting when the working day ends?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Miles schedules delivery vans, our two children are grown and live elsewhere, and there's still a mortgage on our house. My pay is below the usual rate, we have about three weeks of expenses saved, and there aren't many other electrical firms nearby. The wages cover ordinary costs, but a boiler repair is due and a short paid week would put us behind. Retirement is something we talk about over the washing up, not a date backed by confirmed income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a small useful tool can stay without everybody making speeches over lunch. I'd rather hear whether Friday is a full paid day. We still have houses with damaged fittings whether the computer story is large or small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be relieved about the trade carrying on, but our money would still be tight. Three weeks saved doesn't make the boiler repair comfortable, and a short paid week could leave the mortgage account short. Few nearby firms means I can't treat another job as something sitting in a drawer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'd cancel the monthly sports television package, which costs 20 and has no cancellation charge, and put that money toward the boiler bill. I'd keep my present paid repair work through the next year, using the usual electrical checks and occasional checked AI explanations. I wouldn't buy a new course or count on either grown child paying the bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the ordinary week, with some relief that the job itself isn't being overturned. I'd still listen for the boiler clicking off at home. A quiet AI year wouldn't mend our boiler or add another wage day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Miles about cancelling the television?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'd rather miss a match than put the repair on a card we couldn't clear. We already watch more of the highlights than the whole game. It's a real monthly cost I can stop, not a claim that 20 will solve retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does having a licence make another job easy to find?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The licence shows I'm allowed to do my work, not that a nearby employer has a vacancy. I'm experienced and competent at ordinary jobs, but I'm not a specialist somebody is chasing. I'd need an actual offer before treating another wage as ours.

I'd ask about **Friday's paid hours** while the ordinary repair jobs still need doing.
think: Our **three-week reserve** leaves the boiler repair and a short paid week worrying even without radical AI change.
My **electrician's licence** doesn't create a vacancy among the few nearby employers.
do: Cancel the **20 monthly television package** without a cancellation charge and redirect the money to the boiler bill.
Keep **present paid repair work** through the next year, retaining electrical checks and occasional checked AI explanations.
feel: **Anxious with some relief**, still exposed to an ordinary short wage week and the boiler repair.
S0.quote: A quiet AI year wouldn't mend our boiler or add another wage day.
fieldNote: Her **baseline money pressure** persists in Plateau; current wages cover ordinary costs, but the reserve and local job choice are thin.
Her **licence and experience** support ordinary electrical work, without implying specialist skill, crew leadership or an available alternative job.

steps.text: Cancel the 20 monthly television package without fees and redirect the money to the boiler bill
Keep present paid repair work with electrical checks and occasional checked AI explanations

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say quicker booking doesn't automatically mean a fitter can finish an old building any quicker. I'd ask two workmates whether they'd join a clear request about the paid rota. We can like working for our money and still ask what the paid week will be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Miles does planning and booking all day, so his delivery scheduling could lose hours before my physical repair work. My own paid days could shrink if the office squeezed jobs into fewer visits. With three weeks saved and low pay, I can't afford to call either possibility somebody else's problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cancel the same fee-free 20 monthly television package for the boiler bill. Now I'd ask two workmates to agree and sign a joint request for a written paid rota before we sent that exact wording to the employer. During the first year I'd practise the approved AI note-sorting aid after a colleague demonstrated it, only free inside paid shifts with normal weekly wages maintained. I'd check every reordered note against the original job sheet before using it, rather than ask the program to decide an electrical test.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about two wages, and a little less alone if the others want the same clear answer. I'd like trying a small proven tool more than arguing about whether I ought to like change. The mortgage account doesn't distinguish between my missing hours and my partner's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the other electricians don't want their names on the request?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I wouldn't send a letter pretending to speak for them. I'd ask my own question about my own paid week. A joint request needs willing people and agreed words, not just my impatience.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would an invitation to learn the aid be enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not if learning meant an unpaid evening or buying access myself. I'd ask for the demonstration inside the paid day with the normal weekly wage unchanged. Until that was agreed I'd use the existing notes, which I can already check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew the first date is thinking work, not a robot at every socket. I'd be 60 in 2028 and 63 when the capable robots followed around 2031. Miles's scheduling work faces the first date much more directly than my hands-on repairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect most of Miles's scheduling wage to go around 2028, and that would leave a hole my low pay wouldn't cover. Then I could lose physical repair hours when robots followed. I'd be awake adding the mortgage and the boiler bill, knowing three weeks saved isn't a bridge across an unconfirmed retirement income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The fee-free 20 monthly television package would stay cancelled for the boiler bill, and now I'd request available free evening community advice on actual resource eligibility, amounts and dates. I'd apply for posted local electrical maintenance jobs within my licence and actual ability now, and in 2029 if income was still needed. I'd leave my current employer only after a written offer guaranteed pay and paid hours covering essentials after travel, not on the strength of an interview. Advice would need to check real household costs without assuming a pension, an adult child's wage or an affordable stopping date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, because I expect a large household wage loss and I can hear myself doing sums in bed. I can still cancel a bill, apply and ask a sensible question. Being able to act doesn't make the missing wage small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if none of the nearby employers advertised?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the actual paid work available rather than resign to prove I'd started looking. Few local firms can mean a long empty list. An application is something I can choose; a vacancy and a better offer aren't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the advice request need to establish?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The actual eligibility rules, amounts and starting dates, set beside our costs and debts. I'd request an available evening appointment, not assume somebody was already assigned to us. My age doesn't deposit a retirement payment in the mortgage account.

say: I'd separate **2028 thinking work** from capable robots reaching physical repairs around 2031.
I'd name **Miles's scheduling exposure** rather than assume my hands-on timetable protects the whole household.
think: I expect **most scheduling wages** to disappear before later robot pressure on my physical repair hours.
Our **three-week reserve** can't confirm a bridge between lost wages, the mortgage and unknown retirement income.
do: Cancel **20 monthly television** without fees for boiler costs; request available free evening community advice on actual resource eligibility, amounts and dates.
Apply for **posted local electrical maintenance** jobs within licence and ability now, and during 2029 only if income remains needed.
Require a **written offer** guaranteeing pay and paid hours covering essentials after travel before leaving the current employer.
feel: **Alarmed and sleepless**, expecting major household wage loss while retaining concrete applications, cost cuts and advice requests.
S2.quote: My age doesn't deposit a retirement payment in the mortgage account.
fieldNote: Her **first wage shock** concerns Miles's thinking-heavy scheduling around 2028, with physical electrical exposure later around 2031.
Her **applications** are actual chosen searches, not promised vacancies, signed offers or a claim that her licence guarantees hiring.

steps.text: Request available free evening advice on actual resource eligibility, amounts, dates and household costs

Leave only after a written offer guarantees pay and paid hours covering essentials after travel
Cancel the 20 monthly television package without fees for the boiler bill

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us more time to find the actual figures, not five years of free money. I'd be 63 at thinking AGI and 66 around the robot date. I'd keep the practical work separate from Miles's planning work when we talked about whose wage changed first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still worry about a shorter paid week now, before the big dates, with so little saved. I expect a large loss of Miles's scheduling wage around 2031, and not knowing what would replace it would keep me awake. A few more years give us time to check an answer rather than make the expected hole harmless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cancel the same fee-free 20 monthly television package for the boiler bill and request available free evening advice now on actual resources, conditions and dates. I'd keep the current paid repair work while we checked those figures. In 2032 we'd review confirmed resources, actual costs, my ability and real paid options with Miles before deciding whether stopping was affordable and jointly agreed. I'd assume neither a job at 64 nor retirement money or wages from our grown children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed about the expected household income loss, though less rushed about where to ask first. The boiler bill doesn't wait for 2031, and I wouldn't sleep well just because the card moved the larger threat back. I'd rather hear an awkward number early than a pleasant guess late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the first advice meeting decide when you could stop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only actual figures and conditions could support that decision, and an available meeting might leave questions unanswered. I'd ask what still needed checking instead of hearing the word retirement as a promise. Miles and I would both need to agree that the real costs were covered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you explain the plan to your grown children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them what we'd checked without sending them an invoice for the difference. They have their own households, and I haven't asked for or been offered a regular payment. Keeping family close isn't the same as writing their wages into our account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell friends I still need a sensible paid day now, whatever somebody predicts about older workers. I'd be 68 in 2036 and around 71 at the robot date. I'd welcome the time to check a choice without telling everybody my age had already made one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The distant date makes the technology question less urgent, but not the boiler bill or the chance of a short paid week. Miles's scheduling could face pressure before full AGI, and my low pay leaves little room to replace his hours. I don't know our actual later income or whether I'd have the body and an offer for paid work at 69.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep current paid repair work and ask for paired access on awkward loft jobs during normal paid shifts, with normal weekly wages maintained, rather than pretend experience makes every reach safe. I'd request available free evening advice now and review actual household records yearly with Miles, sooner if either wage fell. In 2037 we'd check confirmed resources, actual costs, ability and real paid options before any exit, requiring affordability and Miles's agreement. The television would stay cancelled under the ordinary budget; I'd assume no pension date or unoffered help from our children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the household's actual paid weeks, with less dread about the full AGI date itself. I could enjoy repairing a neat row of lights without believing I must do ladders forever. Having more years to ask doesn't make three weeks saved a comfortable cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does asking for paired loft access mean the firm will agree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd ask for a safe paid arrangement and discuss what jobs could actually be assigned. I wouldn't fill an unsafe gap with enthusiasm, and I wouldn't count an unagreed arrangement as paid hours. The request is about doing today's work safely, not buying a promise about my body ten years on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the 2037 figures still didn't cover stopping?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd use the actual shortfall and available advice to check real options then. I'd count only work actually offered within my ability and help actually agreed, not a child's imagined spare bedroom or a made-up pension. A long career doesn't make every later year affordable.

My **later ability and income** remain unknown, regardless of today's electrical experience.

fieldNote: Her **safe-work request** seeks an employer agreement, without assuming approved staffing or lifelong physical work capacity.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I expect most of Miles's scheduling wage to go before we have confirmed another income, with robots reaching my physical work later. Clear paid hours, free practical teaching inside the paid day and actual household resource figures would help. I'd rather know which wage pays the mortgage than be told my generation will somehow manage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what an experienced worker can still be unsure about. I know an ordinary repair job, but I don't know what a retirement adviser will find or whether another employer is hiring. I'd like those differences left in the story.

headlineQuote: I'd rather know which wage pays the mortgage than be told my generation will somehow manage.
portrait: Dana, **58**, is an experienced electrician with a vocational certificate and electrician's licence, doing ordinary repairs without crew leadership.
She has **lower pay**, three weeks saved, few nearby firms, a mortgage and delivery-scheduler partner Miles; their children are grown.
She uses **AI occasionally**, trying new note sorting only after demonstration with free paid practice, maintained wages and her own checks.
Her **household plans** separate current costs and partner exposure from unknown retirement resources, future capacity and unoffered family help.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** brings expected loss of most of Miles's scheduling wage before confirmed replacement, with later robot pressure on physical repairs.
whatWouldHelp: **Clear paid hours**, free practical teaching inside the paid day and actual household resource figures would support decisions without generational promises.
